chapter: New Orleans style and bass playing
title: Two beats are Chicago style; four beats and Ram Hall
summary: Garland says two beats came from Chicago and drummers dropped four for tiredness, and praises his rhythm partnership with Minor Hall.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Okay, right, okay. So then we're talking about New Orleans style, it was a four-beat music --
That's right.
That really swung and had that happy feeling.
That's right, that happy feeling is right.

So people in the '40's, in the 1940's were talking about Dixieland, or New Orleans music as a two-beat feeling, and you're always, everytime I talk to you, you're talking about four-beats and Pops was talking about four-beats.
That's right.
And so these guys would talk about two-beats, they're wrong, I guess.
No, no, no. That two-beats you understand, just come on up, around Chicago style, you understand that?
Uh-huh, I see.
That two beats, they come up to them boys, they didn't know nothing about no four-beats. And they claim the drummers used to kick on that four beats on account of the leg, they get tired.
I see.
Yeah, they didn't want to -- the four
beats, you know.
Uh-huh.
They fall down on that. They come off the two beats, some of them with a beat bom-bom-bom- but that's the way, steady it started going.
Yeah.
One-tw-three-four-- one-two-three-four-- one-two-three-four.
Uh-huh.
And bass is bom-bom-bom-bom and that's me and that drummer just right together.
Right.
If I have to say it myself, there ain't me and Rom nobody like round, which is Minor Mina Hall, [went] together on that, couldn't be beat. It was -- that Ram was really a rhythm man. On the drums.
